claim: Auditory receptor neurons of grasshoppers respond to sound in a surprisingly temperature-compensated manner with average Q10 values around 1.5.
source: Auditory receptor neurons of grasshoppers respond to sound in a surprisingly temperature-compensated manner: firing rates depend moderately on temperature, with average Q10 values around 1.5.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of firing rates at different temperatures presented in the manuscript.

claim: Temperature compensation of spike generation can be achieved solely relying on cell-intrinsic processes despite a strong dependence of ion conductances on temperature.
source: Analysis of conductance-based neuron models reveals that temperature compensation of spike generation can be achieved solely relying on cell-intrinsic processes and despite a strong dependence of ion conductances on temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results showing temperature compensation with realistic Q10 values for ion channels.

claim: Temperature compensation need not come at an additional metabolic cost of spike generation.
source: Remarkably, this type of temperature compensation need not come at an additional metabolic cost of spike generation.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of energy consumption across different model parameters.

claim: Firing rate-based information transfer is likely to increase with temperature.
source: Firing rate-based information transfer is likely to increase with temperature and we derive predictions for an optimal temperature dependence of the tympanal transduction process fostering temperature compensation.
evidence: This claim is supported by Fisher information analysis showing that information transfer scales with the slope of the f-I curve, which increases with temperature.

claim: Grasshopper auditory receptor neurons do not receive input from the neuronal network.
source: The absence of network inputs to these receptor neurons (Vogel and Ronacher, 2007; Clemens et al., 2011) suggests that a cellular mechanism underlies the observed temperature compensation and hence raises the more general question to what extent temperature compensation can be achieved at the level of individual cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Several invertebrate species have firing-rate Q10 values above 2.
source: Several invertebrate species were found to have firing-rate Q10 values above 2 (i.e., to double their neurons' firing rate), which is in line with the fact that many underlying biochemical processes also exhibit Q10 values of two or more (French and Kuster, 1982; Pfau et al., 1989; Warzecha et al., 1999; Hille, 2001; Spavieri et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Grasshopper auditory receptor neurons increased their firing rate by only ~40-50% (corresponding to a Q10 value of 1.4-1.5).
source: In contrast, we found that grasshopper auditory receptor neurons on average increased their firing rate by only ∼40–50% (corresponding to a Q10 value of 1.4–1.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements presented in the study.

claim: Receptor responses are shaped by a cascade of two major steps: auditory transduction and spike generation.
source: Receptor responses are shaped by a cascade of two major steps (Gollisch and Herz, 2005)—(1) auditory transduction, which translates the vibrations of the tympanal membrane into receptor currents and (2) spike generation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work and represents established knowledge about sensory processing.

claim: Energy efficiency of signaling is an important constraint for neural systems.
source: As energy efficiency of signaling is an important constraint (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Niven and Laughlin, 2008), we also resolve whether the identified mechanisms for temperature compensation come at an additional metabolic cost and identify the key parameters of temperature dependence that increase energy efficiency of action-potential generation as well as of the maintenance of the resting potential.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on neural energy efficiency.

claim: At a given temperature, the transfer function (firing rate as a function of sound intensity) has a sigmoidal shape.
source: At a given temperature, the transfer function, that is the firing rate as a function of sound intensity, has a sigmoidal shape (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Three parameters (saturation rate, half-max sound level, and dynamic-range width) are sufficient to capture the experimental transfer functions with R2 >0.95 for all response curves.
source: Three parameters (saturation rate, half-max sound level, and dynamic-range width) are sufficient to capture the experimental transfer functions (R2 >0.95 for all response curves).
evidence: This claim is supported by the quality of fits to experimental data.

claim: All corresponding median Q10 values for transfer function parameters were below 1.5.
source: Comparing transfer functions at the two different temperatures revealed that their temperature dependence was surprisingly low (Figure 1C): all corresponding median Q10 values were below 1.5
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The sound intensity at half-maximal response (half-max sound level) remained almost unchanged with temperature.
source: the sound intensity at half-maximal response (half-max sound level) remained almost unchanged, as did the median of the slope at half-max sound level.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of transfer function parameters at different temperatures.

claim: The width of action potentials was lower at the higher temperature.
source: The width of action potentials, in contrast, was lower at the higher temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1.

claim: The grasshopper auditory periphery consists of a relatively simple feed-forward network in which the receptor neurons constitute the first layer.
source: The grasshopper auditory periphery consists of a relatively simple feed-forward network, in which the receptor neurons constitute the first layer.
evidence: This claim represents established anatomical knowledge about the grasshopper auditory system.

claim: Approximately 80 receptor neurons converge to ~15 local neurons, which in turn project to ~20 ascending neurons in the grasshopper auditory system.
source: approximately 80 receptor neurons converge to ∼15 local neurons, which in turn project to ∼20 ascending neurons (Vogel and Ronacher, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous anatomical work.

claim: The Connor-Stevens model was used to simulate a type I spike generation process as assumed for grasshopper receptor neurons.
source: We used the Connor–Stevens model (Connor et al., 1977; Dayan and Abbott, 2005) to simulate a type I spike generation process (Izhikevich, 2007) as it is assumed for grasshopper receptor neurons (Benda, 2002).
evidence: This claim describes the modeling approach and is supported by citations to the model and its application.

claim: The Connor-Stevens model comprises a sodium conductance, a leak conductance, a delayed-rectifier potassium conductance, and an A-type potassium conductance.
source: Besides a sodium and a leak conductance (gNa and gL), this model comprises a delayed-rectifier and an A-type potassium conductance (gK and gA), which are both known to be present in the grasshopper nervous system (Ramirez et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim describes the model structure and is supported by a citation confirming the presence of these conductances in grasshoppers.

claim: Temperature dependence parameters were varied within physiologically realistic ranges: Q10(x)∈[2.0,4.0] for transition rates and Q10(ḡX)∈[1.2,2.0] for peak conductances.
source: For a systematic analysis (refers to (Prinz et al., 2003)), we independently varied the temperature dependence of these parameters (comprising a total of nine) within physiologically realistic ranges: Q10(x)∈[2.0,4.0] for transition rates and Q10(g¯X)∈[1.2,2.0] for peak conductances (Partridge and Connor, 1978; Hille, 2001).
evidence: This claim describes the parameter ranges used in the modeling study, supported by citations to physiological literature.

claim: Across all model combinations, the relative change (RMSD) was distributed between 0.22 and 2.14, with a median of 0.68.
source: Across all model combinations, the relative change, RMSD, was distributed between 0.22 and 2.14, with a median of 0.68 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: 18% of models exhibited temperature compensation with relative changes in firing rate comparable to those found experimentally (RMSD <0.5).
source: A fraction of models (18%) exhibited temperature compensation with relative changes in firing rate comparable to those found experimentally (RMSD <0.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results analyzing the distribution of RMSD values.

claim: The largest impact on the RMSD was exerted by three parameters of potassium channels: temperature dependence of the delayed-rectifier potassium kinetics (Q10(n)), and the A-type and delayed-rectifier potassium peak conductances (Q10(ḡA) and Q10(ḡK)).
source: The analysis revealed that the largest impact on the RMSD was exerted by three parameters of potassium channels: temperature dependence of the delayed-rectifier potassium kinetics, Q10(n), and the A-type and delayed-rectifier potassium peak conductances, Q10(g¯A) and Q10(g¯K), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The impacts of both potassium channel peak conductances were negative (increases in their Q10 values decreased the RMSD), while the potassium activation Q10(n) had a positive impact.
source: The impacts of both potassium channel peak conductances were negative (i.e., increases in their Q10 values decreased the RMSD), while the potassium activation Q10(n) had a positive impact (i.e., increases in its temperature dependence increased the RMSD).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis results.

claim: The impact ranking was robust against ±20% perturbations of the model's peak conductances at 18°C.
source: The impact ranking across those models was highly similar to the ranking in the original Connor–Stevens model (Figure 2E) and we conclude that our results are robust.
evidence: This claim is supported by robustness analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A structurally different Traub-Miles model showed that an equally low temperature dependence is possible.
source: Moreover, we note that our results are not unique to the Connor–Stevens model. An analysis of a structurally different Traub–Miles model (Traub et al., 1991; Benda, 2002) showed that an equally low temperature dependence is possible (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by additional modeling results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: With heating, the slope of the f-I curve always increased.
source: With heating, the slope always increased (Figure 2G), while we found changes in both directions for the threshold (Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Temperature dependencies of the A-type potassium and leak peak conductances had the strongest influence on the threshold.
source: Temperature dependencies of the A-type potassium and leak peak conductances had the strongest influence on the threshold (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The slope was most sensitive to the temperature dependence of the delayed-rectifier potassium channel (Q10(n) and Q10(ḡK)) and the sodium channel inactivation (Q10(h)).
source: In contrast, the slope was most sensitive to the temperature dependence of the delayed-rectifier potassium channel, Q10(n) and Q10(g¯K), and the sodium channel inactivation, Q10(h) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Temperature compensation was usually achieved by modest increases in threshold balancing the effects of an increase in slope.
source: Beyond clarifying the specific effect of the aforementioned parameters on changes to the f-I curve, the analysis shows that temperature compensation (i.e., lower RMSD values) was usually achieved by modest increases in threshold balancing the effects of an increase in slope (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of f-I curve changes shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Information transfer scales with the slope of the f-I curve and its temperature dependence hence with Q10(A)^4.
source: Considering the average information transferred for a given interval of firing rates [fmin, fmax], information transfer scales with the slope of the f-I curve and its temperature dependence hence with Q10(A)4 ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This claim is derived from Fisher information analysis detailed in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Overall, heating was advantageous for information transfer.
source: Overall, heating was advantageous for information transfer (Figure 2K).
evidence: This claim is supported by Fisher information analysis results shown in Figure 2K.

claim: In the grasshopper auditory periphery firing rates often exceed several hundreds of Hz, suggesting that metabolic cost may have played a role in the design of these cells.
source: In the grasshopper auditory periphery firing rates often exceed several hundreds of Hz, suggesting that metabolic cost may have played a role in the design of these cells.
evidence: This claim combines experimental observation with inference about evolutionary constraints.

claim: For the majority of models (93%), the energetic cost of an action potential decreased with heating.
source: For the majority of models, the energetic cost of an action potential decreased with heating (93% of models, Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of energy consumption shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Temperature-compensated spike generation models were slightly more costly than the most temperature-dependent models on average.
source: On average, temperature-compensated spike generation models (25% of models with lowest RMSD) were slightly more costly than the most temperature-dependent models (25% of models with highest RMSD), see Figure 3B.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis comparing energy costs across model subgroups shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The minimum energy consumption was comparable in both temperature-compensated and strongly temperature-dependent model groups.
source: Nevertheless, the minimum energy consumption was comparable in both groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of energy consumption distributions.

claim: Sodium-current based resting cost tended to decrease with heating (77% of models).
source: Sodium-current based resting cost tended to decrease with heating (77% of models).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of resting potential energy costs.

claim: The temperature-dependence of the sodium conductance (Q10(h) and Q10(ḡNa)) influenced energy consumption of spike generation the most.
source: The sensitivity analysis (performed in analogy to the analysis of temperature dependence of firing rate) revealed that the temperature-dependence of the sodium conductance (Q10(h) and Q10(g¯Na)) influenced energy consumption of spike generation the most (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The key parameters of largest influence on temperature compensation and energy efficiency belonged to different channel groups: potassium channels for temperature compensation and sodium channels for energy efficiency of spike generation.
source: In particular, the key parameters of largest influence on these features belonged to different channel groups: potassium channels in case of temperature compensation and sodium channels in case of energy efficiency of spike generation.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing sensitivity analysis results for RMSD and energy consumption.

claim: Striving for temperature compensation does not have to compromise a neuron's energy efficiency.
source: In summary, striving for temperature compensation does not have to compromise a neuron's energy efficiency.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis showing that temperature compensation and energy efficiency can be achieved simultaneously.

claim: Little is known about the temperature dependence of transduction in the grasshopper.
source: Little is known about the temperature dependence of transduction in the grasshopper.
evidence: This claim represents a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The largest temperature dependence of the 'matching' transduction curves was to be expected for their dynamic-range width (median Q10 ~2).
source: Evaluating the distribution of changes of the ideal transduction curves with temperature across all spike generation models, we found that the largest temperature dependence of these 'matching' transduction curves was to be expected for their dynamic-range width (median Q10∼2).
evidence: This claim is supported by reverse-engineering analysis of transduction curves.

claim: Changes in saturation current and half-maximum sound level also contributed to fostering temperature compensation of firing rate.
source: In addition, changes in saturation current and half-maximum sound level also contributed to fostering temperature compensation of firing rate (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by reverse-engineering analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A suitable temperature dependence of the transduction process can support temperature compensation, even in cases where spike generation is less temperature robust.
source: These results show in particular that a suitable temperature dependence of the transduction process can support temperature compensation, even in cases where spike generation is less temperature robust.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the reverse-engineering analysis of transduction curves.

claim: Neurons in the auditory periphery of grasshoppers show Q10 values on the order of 1.5 and are remarkably temperature compensated.
source: It was hence surprising to observe that neurons in the auditory periphery of grasshoppers show Q10 values on the order of 1.5 and consequently are remarkably temperature compensated (Hazel and Prosser, 1974; Boulant and Dean, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements and citations to literature on temperature compensation.

claim: The temperature robustness of grasshopper auditory neurons is comparable to that of 'warm-insensitive' neurons in the mammalian brain.
source: The temperature robustness of these neurons is hence comparable to that of 'warm-insensitive' neurons in the mammalian brain (Curras and Boulant, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with cited literature on mammalian neurons.

claim: Temperature compensation in grasshopper receptor neurons must be based on cell-intrinsic processes.
source: Temperature compensation in grasshopper receptor neurons, by comparison, must be based on cell-intrinsic processes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the absence of network inputs to these neurons.

claim: A similar temperature compensation based on a single-cell mechanism has been described experimentally for tarsal hairs in the locust.
source: A similar temperature compensation that must be based on a single-cell mechanism has so far—to our knowledge—only been described experimentally for tarsal hairs in the locust (Miles, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Phenomenologically, a rise in slope is compensated for by an increase in the threshold of the f-I curve, minimizing the effect of temperature across a broader range of inputs.
source: Phenomenologically, a rise in slope (consistent across the whole parameter range explored) is compensated for by an increase in the threshold of the f-I curve, minimizing the effect of temperature across a broader range of inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results analyzing f-I curve changes.

claim: Alterations in threshold can be produced by changes in peak conductances of ion channels and have been described experimentally by heating in invertebrate systems.
source: While alterations in threshold can be produced by changes in peak conductances of ion channels, they have also been described experimentally by heating in invertebrate systems (Burkhardt, 1959; Abrams and Pearson, 1982; Kispersky et al., 2012) in agreement with our observations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental literature.

claim: The temperature dependence of both delayed-rectifier and A-type potassium channels has a particularly large impact on temperature compensation, which matches experimental observations in neurons of the pancreas of mice and molluscan neurons.
source: The temperature dependence of both delayed-rectifier and A-type potassium channels has a particularly large impact on temperature compensation. This matches experimental observations in neurons of the pancreas of mice (Xu et al., 2006) and molluscan neurons as well as previous simulations of an extended Hodgkin–Huxley model (Rush and Rinzel, 1995)
evidence: This claim is supported by computational results and citations to experimental and modeling literature.

claim: For auditory receptor neurons in the grasshopper energy efficiency of spike generation is likely to be a relevant factor.
source: For auditory receptor neurons in the grasshopper energy efficiency of spike generation is likely to be a relevant factor, also see Niven and Farris (2012).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the high firing rates observed and is supported by a citation.

claim: The rate of sodium channel inactivation proved to be most relevant in setting the energy consumption per spike generated, which is consistent with simulations and dynamic clamp experiments in various model systems.
source: The rate of sodium channel inactivation (Figure 3D) proved to be most relevant in setting the energy consumption per spike generated, which is consistent with simulations and dynamic clamp experiments in various model systems (Alle et al., 2009; Hasenstaub et al., 2010; Sengupta et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational results and citations to previous studies.

claim: Energy efficiency improved with heating for a wide range of temperature dependencies of ion channels.
source: We demonstrated that energy efficiency improved with heating for a wide range of temperature dependencies of ion channels, as was previously described for a model with fixed Q10 values (Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational results and a citation to previous modeling work.

claim: A fast sodium inactivation limits the duration of the spike, which was consistent with the experimental data showing spike width decreased with heating.
source: A fast sodium inactivation limits the duration of the spike; this was consistent with the experimental data, as spike width decreased with heating.
evidence: This claim connects computational results with experimental observations.

claim: The key parameters regulating the energy efficiency of spiking were different from those regulating temperature compensation of firing rate.
source: Most importantly, the key parameters regulating the energy efficiency of spiking were different from those regulating temperature compensation of firing rate (Figure 2C, Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing sensitivity analysis results shown in Figures 2C and 3D.

claim: From an evolutionary perspective, the relevant features—robustness of firing rate to temperature changes and reduction of metabolic cost—could both be achieved in parallel.
source: Summarizing the considerations on metabolic cost, we find most noteworthy that from an evolutionary perspective, the relevant features—robustness of firing rate to temperature changes and reduction of metabolic cost—could both be achieved in parallel.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the computational results showing independent control of these features.

claim: Higher temperatures are advantageous for the transmission of information about sound intensity.
source: Our sensitivity analysis revealed that higher temperatures are also advantageous for the transmission of information about sound intensity.
evidence: This claim is supported by Fisher information analysis.

claim: The capacity to transmit information was affected most by the temperature dependence of the delayed-rectifier potassium conductance.
source: This conclusion is based on our finding that the slope of the f-I curve increased with heating. The capacity to transmit information was affected most by the temperature dependence of the delayed-rectifier potassium conductance.
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis of Fisher information.

claim: All auditory input passes through the peripheral network, which preprocesses information and extracts behaviorally-relevant features.
source: All auditory input passes through this peripheral network, which preprocesses information and extracts behaviorally-relevant features (Clemens et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on the grasshopper auditory system.

claim: The large investment into high firing rates and a comparatively high redundancy between neurons in the receptor layer increases the need for energy-efficient spike generation.
source: The large investment into high firing rates and a comparatively high redundancy between neurons in this layer (Machens et al., 2001) also increases the need for energy-efficient spike generation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed properties of the system and is supported by a citation.

claim: Optimization of receptor neurons in terms of temperature compensation seems a reasonable 'strategy', as all effects of temperature on receptor neurons will be passed on to downstream neurons, where they may multiply.
source: Optimization of receptor neurons in terms of temperature compensation hence seems a reasonable 'strategy', as all effects of temperature on receptor neurons will be passed on to downstream neurons, where they may multiply.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about evolutionary strategy based on the system architecture.

claim: Downstream neurons may adopt different strategies including balancing of inhibition and excitation for robustness to temperature changes as well as an increase in population and temporal sparseness for energy efficiency and information transfer.
source: Downstream neurons, in contrast, may be expected to adopt different strategies, as they can make use of different mechanisms: balancing of inhibition and excitation for robustness to temperature changes (Robertson and Money, 2012) as well as an increase in population and temporal sparseness for energy efficiency and information transfer (Clemens et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is a speculation supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: A slight shift of transduction to lower sound intensities with higher temperatures may be favorable for temperature compensation.
source: Our computational analysis shows that, indeed, a slight shift of transduction to lower sound intensities with higher temperatures may be favorable.
evidence: This claim is supported by reverse-engineering analysis of transduction curves.

claim: A shift in transduction to lower sound intensities would occur if the amplitude of the tympanal vibration increased with heating and a stimulus of given intensity hence opened more transduction channels.
source: Such a shift would occur if the amplitude of the tympanal vibration increased with heating and a stimulus of given intensity hence opened more transduction channels.
evidence: This claim is a mechanistic explanation inferred from the modeling results.

claim: The computationally-derived changes in transduction parameters are relatively moderate, which is consistent with the observation that the tympanal vibration in cicadas is relatively temperature independent.
source: However, the computationally-derived changes are relatively moderate (Figure 4D). This is consistent with the observation that the tympanal vibration in cicadas is relatively temperature independent (Fonseca and Correia, 2007).
evidence: This claim connects computational predictions with experimental observations from cicadas cited in the literature.

claim: The increase in dynamic-range width with heating can be interpreted as a decrease in gating force in a gating-spring model for the transduction as proposed for mechanosensory transduction in bullfrog saccular hair cells.
source: The increase in dynamic-range width with heating can be interpreted as a decrease in gating force in a gating-spring model for the transduction as proposed for mechanosensory transduction in bullfrog saccular hair cells (Howard and Hudspeth, 1988).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of modeling results based on a cited mechanistic model.

claim: Increases in temperature are advantageous because the gating-force magnitude is inversely related to transduction accuracy.
source: Again, increases in temperature are advantageous, because the gating-force magnitude is inversely related to transduction accuracy (van Netten et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on cited literature about transduction accuracy.

claim: Decreases in saturation current with heating may require additional heat-sensitive channels with a modulatory influence on the transduction process, such as thermosensitive transient receptor channels (TRPA).
source: The latter may require additional heat-sensitive channels with a modulatory influence on the transduction process, such as thermosensitive transient receptor channels (TRPA) (Kang et al., 2012), which in principle could down-regulate the saturation level of the transduction function via their increased calcium response (Chadha and Cook, 2012).
evidence: This claim is a speculation about possible mechanisms supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Spike generation alone is sufficient to mediate robustness of the firing rate.
source: Generally, the analysis shows that the transduction process can contribute to temperature compensation. While spike generation alone is sufficient to mediate robustness of the firing rate, a matched temperature dependence of the transduction process may allow for more flexibility in the 'choice' of spike generation parameters, including the possibility to meet additional constraints.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results showing temperature compensation with spike generation alone.

claim: A matched temperature dependence of the transduction process may allow for more flexibility in the 'choice' of spike generation parameters, including the possibility to meet additional constraints.
source: While spike generation alone is sufficient to mediate robustness of the firing rate, a matched temperature dependence of the transduction process may allow for more flexibility in the 'choice' of spike generation parameters, including the possibility to meet additional constraints.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the reverse-engineering analysis.

claim: Auditory receptor neurons in the grasshopper represent an example of remarkable cell-intrinsic temperature compensation in the absence of network effects.
source: Altogether, our data show that auditory receptor neurons in the grasshopper represent an example of remarkable cell-intrinsic temperature compensation in the absence of network effects.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main finding supported by experimental and computational data.

claim: The identified mechanisms for temperature compensation generalize to spike generation in other cell types.
source: The identified mechanisms generalize to spike generation in other cell types.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the generic nature of the modeling approach.

claim: Additional nonlinear processing by static nonlinearities may foster temperature compensation if well matched with the temperature dependence of spike generation.
source: Moreover, additional nonlinear processing by static nonlinearities (here interpreted as the transduction process involving the tympanal membrane, but on a wider scope also reflecting properties of synaptic transmission) may foster temperature compensation, if well matched with the temperature dependence of spike generation.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the reverse-engineering analysis that generalizes beyond the specific system.

claim: The dependence of neuronal processing on temperature merits further investigation, in particular as temperature fluctuations are an oftentimes underestimated variable in mammalian systems too.
source: Overall, the dependence of neuronal processing on temperature merits further investigation, in particular as temperature fluctuations are an oftentimes underestimated variable in mammalian systems too.
evidence: This claim is a statement about the broader significance of the work.

claim: Experiments were performed on adult Locusta migratoria obtained from a commercial supplier and held at room temperature (22–25°C).
source: Experiments were performed on adult L. migratoria, obtained from a commercial supplier and held at room temperature (22–25°C).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods.

claim: Intracellular recordings from auditory neurons within the metathoracic ganglion were conventionally conducted using glass microelectrodes filled with a 3–5% solution of Lucifer yellow in 0.5 M LiCl.
source: Intracellular recordings from auditory neurons within the metathoracic ganglion were conventionally conducted as described elsewhere (Franz and Ronacher, 2002; Wohlgemuth and Ronacher, 2007), using glass microelectrodes filled with a 3–5% solution of Lucifer yellow in 0.5 M LiCl.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methods with citations to previous work.

claim: For each experiment, recordings were conducted first at a fixed higher tissue temperature (in the range of 28–29°C), then the preparation was cooled down to a lower temperature (in the range of 21–23°) and recordings were repeated.
source: For each experiment, recordings were conducted first at a fixed higher tissue temperature (in the range of 28–29°C), then the preparation was cooled down to a lower temperature (in the range of 21–23°) and recordings were repeated.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings started 3–5 min after induction of the temperature change.
source: In order not to underestimate Q10 values, we took a conservative approach: Electrophysiological recordings started 3–5 min after induction of the temperature change.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental protocol.

claim: The estimated Q10 values constitute an upper bound and real Q10 values may be slightly smaller (even more temperature compensated).
source: Consequently, the estimated Q10 values constitute an upper bound. In contrast, we cannot exclude that real Q10 values may even be slightly smaller, that is even more temperature compensated.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the interpretation of the experimental measurements.

claim: Nine receptor neurons were recorded in eight preparations.
source: Altogether, nine receptor neurons were recorded in eight preparations.
evidence: This claim describes the sample size of the experimental study.

claim: Acoustic broad band stimuli (100 ms duration, 1–40 kHz bandwidth) repeated five times each at 8 intensities, rising from 32 to 88 dB SPL were used to obtain spike rate vs intensity curves.
source: To obtain spike rate vs intensity curves (response curves), we used acoustic broad band stimuli (100 ms duration, 1–40 kHz bandwidth) repeated five times each at 8 intensities, rising from 32 to 88 dB SPL.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental stimulation protocol.

claim: The model response curves r=φ(θ(IdB)) matched the experimental representative response curve very well (R2 >0.98 for 99.5% of all models).
source: The model response curves r=ϕ(θ(IdB)) matched the experimental representative response curve very well (R2 >0.98 for 99.5% of all models).
evidence: This claim is supported by the quality of fits in the reverse-engineering analysis.
